title: Null, undefined, and three valued logic in SQL: NULL is not equal to NULL
story:
Tony Hoare gave a talk called Null References: The Billion Dollar Mistake at QCon London in March 2009, tracing the null reference to 1965, when he was designing the first comprehensive type system for references in an object-oriented language. The detail worth keeping is his account of why it is there. His goal had been that all use of references should be absolutely safe, with checking performed automatically by the compiler. He added the null reference simply because it was so easy to implement.

That is a more interesting admission than the headline. The mistake was not a failure of foresight about consequences; it was a small local convenience admitted into a design whose explicit purpose was to make that class of error impossible. The feature that undermined the guarantee was cheap, and cheap is how it got in.

The database version of the problem is worse than the language version, because it is quieter. SQL does not use two-valued logic for expressions involving NULL. It uses a three-valued logic whose values are true, false and unknown.

Comparing anything to NULL, including NULL itself, yields unknown rather than true or false. The reasoning is sound once stated: NULL represents the absence of a known value rather than a value, and two unknown quantities cannot be asserted to be equal. If you do not know one person's salary and you do not know another's, you cannot conclude the salaries match — and you cannot conclude they differ either.

Now the rule that turns this from a curiosity into a source of silent wrong answers. A row is returned by a query only when its condition evaluates to true. A condition evaluating to unknown excludes the row exactly as a false one would.

So a filter selecting rows whose status is not some particular value will not return the rows whose status is absent. Those rows are neither in the result nor in the result of the opposite query, because both conditions evaluate to unknown for them. The two halves of what looks like an exhaustive split do not cover everything, and nothing reports this. The query runs, returns rows, and the count is simply lower than it should be — which is why these are typically found months later by someone reconciling totals.

The practical consequences are worth listing because they follow from the same rule and are rarely connected. A negated comparison drops the absent rows. An aggregate that averages a column ignores them rather than treating them as zero, which is usually right and occasionally not what was intended. A join on a column containing NULL does not match, so rows disappear from a join that looks complete. And the only correct way to test for absence is the dedicated operator, because comparing to NULL with the equality operator can never be true.

The defence is structural rather than vigilant. Where a column has no meaning when absent, forbid it from being absent — a constraint is checked by the database on every write, which is worth more than any amount of care in queries written later by people who will not remember. Where absence is genuinely meaningful, handle it explicitly at every point the column is used, and treat any condition on that column as needing a decision about what the absent case should do.

One thing worth being clear about, since the usual framing is that null is simply a mistake. The three-valued logic is not the error; it is the correct treatment of genuinely missing information, and a system that silently substituted a default would be worse, because it would produce confident wrong answers instead of propagating the uncertainty. What Hoare identified is narrower and more precise: making absence indistinguishable in syntax from a value, so that expressions which look like comparisons are not comparisons — and code written as though they were is wrong in a way that generates no error at all.

problem.name: Absence is not a value
problem.shape: A column or reference may hold no value, and code treats it as though it holds one.
tell: a negated condition returns fewer rows than expected
two opposite filters do not sum to the total
a comparison to the absence marker uses the equality operator
problem.move: Forbid absence wherever the column has no meaning without a value, so the database enforces it on every write. Where absence is meaningful, test for it with the dedicated operator and decide explicitly what every condition on that column should do when the value is missing.
problem.invariant: Comparing to the absence marker yields unknown, and a row is returned only when its condition is true — so unknown excludes a row exactly as false does, and two opposite conditions can both exclude the same row.
problem.breaks: The three-valued logic is not the mistake. It is the correct handling of genuinely missing information, and substituting a default would be worse — confident wrong answers instead of propagated uncertainty. The error is narrower: absence shares its syntax with values, so expressions that look like comparisons are not.

cost.time: every condition on a nullable column needs an explicit decision about the absent case
cost.beats: forbidding absence everywhere, which is simplest and cannot represent genuinely unknown data, and substituting a sentinel value, which restores two-valued logic and makes the unknown indistinguishable from a real measurement

worked.reasoning:
Because the comparison does not evaluate to true or false for those rows — it evaluates to unknown, and a row is returned only when its condition is true.

SQL does not use two-valued logic for expressions involving the absence marker. It uses a three-valued logic whose values are true, false and unknown, and comparing anything to the absence marker, including the marker itself, yields unknown. The reasoning is sound: it represents the absence of a known value rather than a value, and two unknown quantities cannot be asserted to be equal — nor to differ. Then the rule that converts this from a curiosity into silent wrong answers: a row appears in the result only when its condition is true, so a condition evaluating to unknown excludes the row exactly as a false condition would.

Which produces the effect worth emphasising. The rows with an absent status are in neither the result of the filter nor the result of its opposite. Two conditions that look like an exhaustive split of the table do not cover it, and nothing reports the gap — the query succeeds, returns rows, and the count is simply lower than it should be. Where a column has no meaning without a value, forbid absence with a constraint, so the database enforces it on every write — that is worth far more than vigilance in queries written later by people who will not remember. Where absence is genuinely meaningful, decide explicitly what each condition on that column should do.

I would add the point that the usual framing gets wrong. The three-valued logic is not the mistake; it is the correct treatment of genuinely missing information, and a system that silently substituted a default would be worse, because it would produce confident wrong answers instead of propagating uncertainty. Hoare's identification is narrower: he traced the null reference to 1965, when designing the first comprehensive type system for references, with the goal that all reference use be absolutely safe and checked automatically by the compiler — and he added it simply because it was so easy to implement. The error is that absence was given the same syntax as a value, so expressions that look like comparisons are not comparisons, and code written as though they were is wrong in a way that produces no error at all.

problem.practice: Take a table with a nullable column and run two opposite filters on it, then compare their total to the row count. The difference is the set of rows your application's logic has never accounted for.

beats.broke: Absence was given the same syntax as a value, so expressions that look like comparisons are not comparisons — and code written as though they were is wrong in a way that produces no error.
beats.fix: Treat absence as its own logical state: forbid it where the column is meaningless without a value, and where it is meaningful, test for it with the dedicated operator and decide what each condition should do.
beats.cost: A third truth value propagates through every expression, so conditions that appear exhaustive are not — and the excluded rows are silently dropped rather than reported.
